title: Brand, message and offers
subtitle: Say clearly what you do, in your voice, and sell it simply
intro: A good offer that's poorly explained doesn't sell. Neither does a beautiful brand without a clear offer. In this chapter, you work with Claude to build your value proposition, your brand voice guide and a simple lineup of offers, then bring it all together in a foundation Claude reuses for every piece of copy.

steps.d: Put into one sentence the concrete result your client gets, who it's for, and what makes you credible to promise it.
Describe your tone with real examples: the words you use, the ones you ban and what you never say.
Organize your offers into a simple lineup: an entry offer, a core offer and, if needed, a premium offer.
Bring promise, voice and offers together in a single document that Claude checks before writing anything for you.

prompts.title: The value proposition in 3 versions
prompts.use: When you can't explain what you do in one sentence.
prompts.prompt: You are a copywriter who specializes in service offers. My business: [WHAT YOU DO]. My audience: [YOUR ICP]. The main result I deliver: [RESULT]. My proof: [TESTIMONIAL, EXPERIENCE OR METHOD]. Write 3 value propositions: one very factual, one focused on the problem avoided, one focused on the result. Each version includes a headline of 12 words max and a subheadline of 25 words max. Not allowed: jargon, superlatives, numbers I didn't provide. End with the one you would choose and why.

prompts.title: The brand voice guide
prompts.use: When you've already written copy that sounds like you.
prompts.prompt: I'm attaching copy I wrote that sounds like me: [POSTS, EMAILS, SALES PAGES]. Analyze it like a linguist. Produce a brand voice guide with: 4 personality traits written as “we are… but not…”, my usual sentence length, my recurring expressions, words to ban, how I open and close, and a table of 5 examples of “avoid” versus “instead.” The guide must fit on one page so it can serve as a reference.

prompts.title: The offer architect
prompts.use: To clarify your lineup of offers and your prices.
prompts.prompt: Act as an offer consultant for freelancers and small businesses. My current offers: [LIST OF YOUR OFFERS AND PRICES]. Before suggesting anything, ask me 5 questions, one at a time, about: the time each offer takes me, what my clients buy most, what they ask for that I don't sell, my capacity limits and my revenue goal. Then suggest a 3-tier lineup in a table: name, who it's for, promise, content, format, price range to test, role in the lineup. Also tell me what to remove or merge.

prompts.title: The brand guardian
prompts.use: Before you publish, to check that a piece of copy sounds like you.
prompts.prompt: You are the guardian of my brand. Here is my voice guide: [PASTE YOUR GUIDE OR NAME THE PROJECT FILE]. Here is the copy to review: [YOUR TEXT]. Score it from 1 to 10 on three criteria: clarity of the promise, consistency with my voice, alignment with my offers. Quote every sentence that sounds off, explain why in one line and suggest a rewrite. Don't rewrite the whole text, only the parts that need fixing. Present the result as a list.

workflow.title: Workflow: your reusable brand foundation
workflow.where: A Claude Project, then a Skill
steps: Attach five to ten pieces of copy that sound like you and run “The brand voice guide.”
Write your promise with the first prompt, giving it your ICP sheet from chapter 3.
Clarify your lineup with “The offer architect” and sum up your offers in a one-page table.
Combine promise, voice and offers in a “brand foundation” document added to your Project.
Turn this foundation into a Skill so Claude applies it whenever you ask for marketing copy.

checklist: My value proposition makes sense without me explaining it out loud.
It says who it's for, what result and why they should believe me.
My voice guide has real examples, not just adjectives.
I have a list of words I never use.
Each offer has a clear role in my lineup.
A stranger quickly knows which offer fits their case.
mistake: Common mistake: describing your voice with adjectives like “professional but friendly.” Claude can't do anything with that. Give it real copy and examples of what you refuse to say.
tip: Dr. Firas's tip: when you fix a piece of copy from Claude, ask it to add the rule to your voice guide. Week after week, it really starts writing like you.
